sections.text: And if thou are not strong enough to practise concentration, then devote thyself to My service, do all thine acts for My sake, and thou shalt still attain the goal.
And if thou art too weak even for this, then seek refuge in union with Me, and with perfect self-control renounce the fruit of thy action.
Knowledge is superior to blind action, meditation to mere knowledge, renunciation of the fruit of action to meditation, and where there is renunciation peace will follow.

We have been discussing Chapter 12, Bhakti yoga, the Yoga of Devotion. In our scriptures, generally there are three paths prescribed: karma Yoga, Gnana Yoga, and Bhakti Yoga. Most people consider Bhakti Yoga to be the easiest path because it requires no special training, no special arrangement.
You can just go and worship the Lord. You go to the temple, you sing bhajans. So most people feel it is more comfortable and much easier to practice Bhakti yoga than karma Yoga or Gnana Yoga.
Thats our general understanding. But it turns out Bhakti Yoga is the most difficult path to follow, because Bhakti is the emotional response to something we adore or something we worship. Devotion, as we have discussed before, is nothing but love for the divine.
Narad Ji defines Bhakti in his Narad Bhakti Sutra as Sa Tasmin Premarupa -- it is of the nature of love. It is the nature of immortality. Yat labdhva puman siddho bhavati -- once a person achieves that Bhakti, becomes established in Bhakti Yoga, that person becomes Siddha, accomplished.
Amritva bhavati -- he becomes immortal. And Tripto bhavati -- he becomes completely satisfied. So to achieve that state is not very simple.
So what we find actually is it is easier for me to practice karma Yoga. Karma Yoga is something related to my actions. I consider it is in my control.
How I act in this world is something I can control. So Karma Yoga is related to my organs of actions and how I perform my actions in this world which I consider I have some control over it. At least I can attempt to practice Karma Yoga.
And then Gnana Yoga is related to the intellect -- acquiring knowledge. That again I find is something in my control. I can make a choice that I want to learn this or that.
If I want to learn about physics, I can make a resolve, go to the physics department, learn physics. So knowledge is something I find within my choice to pursue, just as actions are within my choice to pursue. But Bhakti is related to the mind.
Its an emotional response. Nobody can say, Ill fall in love in 2025. You cannot plan falling in love. It really does not go by your planning or your calendar.
The love will only come if I know the divine. And therefore, we have gone through five chapters in this segment, from the 7th through the 11th, to know the Supreme Lord. In chapters 10 and 11, Bhagavan has given Arjuna all the required information -- chapter 10 gave all the Vibhutis in the manifest world, then chapter 11 gave him the total representation of his nature.
If you have been equipped with that level of knowledge, then Bhakti actually becomes an automatic response. However, it is still related to the mind. And therefore Bhagavan starts this chapter by saying, fix your mind onto me.
No matter what amount of knowledge I may have intellectually or how much activity I have performed, it is the mind which decides my next destination. It is the mind which will have the desire to explore new things. So Bhagavan said, attach your mind to me.
We have seen in the last few verses that Bhagavan has clarified: focusing your mind on one particular form is the easiest way to do it. That does not mean Bhagavan is simply saying idol worship is all you have to do. So we discussed last time whether idol worship is acceptable or not.
It is one form, one means to achieve bhakti. Most of the time when we consider Bhakti, we think simply: He is going to the temple and singing bhajans, so thats the sum total of bhakti. And Bhagavan said, thats not true. It is your mind that matters, not the activity of going to the temple, not the singing.
Used to say, bhajans with noisy instruments -- thats not Bhakti. Bhakti is where the mind penetrates the nature of the Lord and fixes itself to that form. Bhagavan said, the first requirement is: fix your mind onto me.
Your mind and intellect should be firmly established in that supreme knowledge. Thats what weve been learning throughout these last five chapters. Nothing exists other than his self.
What I see through my senses is his lower nature. What I do not see but feel as my own existence, my own consciousness, is his higher nature. I cannot vouch for any other persons consciousness, but I can vouch for my own -- because I feel I exist, and that nobody can take away from me.
This consciousness cannot be displayed in any other way than when I act outside. Then you can say, Hes speaking, hes talking, hes alive. So that is the higher nature. The consciousness which makes this inert equipment function in this world is the higher nature.
If you understood these two, then focus your mind onto me, constantly think about me does not mean you have to drop everything and start thinking about him. But whatever you think, in the back of your mind you should know that he is the enabler of this thought. Without his presence, without this consciousness, this mind cannot even run away in different directions.
At least you should have that as a background thought. Just as in music you have the Shruti playing in the background -- nobody pays attention to the Shruti. But the moment you miss the Shruti, you are done with your bhajan.
If you pay attention to the Shruti, the entire music falls in place. Once you miss it, everything is haywire. Our Shruti should be that I am that Satchitananda -- this consciousness is me.
But when we miss that and ignore that, the music of our life falls apart. Bhagavan said, therefore Mayy aveshita mana, and then Buddhi niveshaya -- place your intellect into me. So now that intellectually we appreciate that Bhagavan is everywhere, that there is nothing that exists without Bhagavan, that everything I see is Bhagavan alone -- now my intellect reminds me every time I transact in this world.
Then no matter what I think about, the party Im dealing with is nothing but his own representation. And Bhagavan said, if you keep that in mind, you will never be able to do anything wrong. You will not be able to perform any crime.
And therefore he says, Nivasishyasi mayyeva ata urdhvam na samshayah. If you constantly keep this thought in your mind and have your intellect constantly remind you that whatever you are dealing with in this world is nothing but his Prakriti, then you will come to me. You will reside in me.
There is no doubt about it. So Bhagavan has clearly clarified: Bhakti is all about mental control, having the mind focused on the supreme reality. We find that actually very difficult, because we all have admitted that controlling the mind is not that easy.
So Bhakti is actually a destination. You start your journey from Karma Yoga. If you have no other training in spirituality and somebody says this is the path, then the easiest path is Karma Yoga, because you can control your actions.
When you purify mind and intellect through action, your intellect becomes ready for knowledge. Then once you get knowledge, you really have to do nothing. You dont have to do anything.
Bhakti will reveal itself automatically in your mind. Its like when you fell in love -- you didnt even realize when you fell in love. You started knowing about her at some point, and you didnt realize when it happened.
There is no timeframe -- you cant say on such and such date I fell in love. I went to a music teacher when I was in my late 40s, and I kept saying, Subhashi, I really have trouble understanding what you are saying. I understand it, but I dont feel it.
Youre telling me Im out of rhythm, but I dont know when Im out of rhythm. When I stopped going to class, at some point I started understanding it -- Im out of scale, Im out of rhythm. And when that happened, I cannot pinpoint when the knowledge of scale and rhythm came. There is no timeline for it.
But it was because of the music classes I took. This is what happens when knowledge matures into skill. So Bhagavan said, all you have to do is purify your mind and intellect.
Put your mind and intellect in me and this will happen automatically. Once you achieve Bhakti, as Narad Muni said, it is Amrita Swarupa. You will have no fear of death.
You will feel Tripta -- completely satisfied. You will have nothing more to achieve in this world. But Bhagavan is very kind and said there are alternates.
If you dont think that is possible for you even after going through the last five chapters, then he said, if you are not capable of controlling your mind, just perform Abhyasa Yoga. Abhyasa Yoga is simply to keep reminding yourself that you are deviating from what you have learned and to try to bring the mind back to its goal. Its constant practice.
Practice makes you perfect. By practice, you can train wild animals in a circus. So obviously you can train your mind.
If wild animals can be trained, your mind can be trained -- its a matter of how much practice you put in. Bhagavan says, just keep practicing. But somebody like me says, Bhagavan, even thats really difficult.
I get so distracted by my thoughts that I even forget to remember that I have to bring my mind back to where it should be. And Bhagavan has already said in chapter seven that all my devotees are Udaraha -- noble people. No matter what level they are, Udara Sarvaivaithi, they are all good people performing good actions. No matter how incomplete they are, no matter how incapable they are of realizing their own self.
But theyre good people. At whatever level you are -- whether at a kindergarten level or a high school level -- you can start your journey towards your goal. Abhyase api asamarthosi matkarma paramo bhava.
Then perform actions for me. But keep in mind that you are doing it for the Lord. In the sense that if I have come to realize that there is nothing but the Lord alone, then whoever I serve, Im serving him.
In your profession, when you serve your clients, keep in mind that the client is nothing but his own representation. You serving him is serving the Lord. You serve other people -- they are also forms of the same Lord.
And therefore Im serving Him. So keep that thought in mind: I am performing all actions for him only. Madartham api karmani kurvan siddhim avapsyasi -- even just by performing actions for me, you can achieve that perfection.
You dont have to meditate. You dont have to do any kind of tapas. But keep performing your actions for me alone, and keep in mind that youre not doing it for yourself.
This limited self has to be removed from the equation. Now I want welfare of all beings. But even that is not possible for some.
You are so self-focused that you cant think about anybody but yourself. What Im doing is for myself or I am the doer -- the ego is so strong. Bhagavan says, Atha etad api ashakto asi -- if you are even incapable of doing so -- then Kartum madyogam ashritah sarva karma phala tyagam. If you cannot perform all actions for me, perform actions for whatever purpose you were performing before -- for accomplishing things, achieving respect in society, your big bank balances, all that.
Continue doing the same thing you are doing. But give up the anxiety for the fruits.

These verses reveal Krishnas extraordinary compassion as a teacher. He offers a descending ladder of practice for aspirants at different levels. Cannot fix your mind on the Divine? Practice concentration (abhyasa). Cannot practice concentration? Perform actions for His sake (mat-karma). Cannot even do that? Simply renounce the fruits of action (sarva-karma-phala-tyagam). The teaching meets us exactly where we are. Verse 12 presents a remarkable hierarchy: Knowledge is superior to blind action, meditation to mere knowledge, renunciation of the fruit of action to meditation, and where there is renunciation peace will follow. The culmination is telling, peace (shanti) comes immediately (anantaram) from letting go of attachment to results.
This is profoundly practical wisdom. Most of our mental suffering comes not from our actions themselves but from our anxious attachment to their outcomes. We plan for the green card, then the partner, then the children, then their education, then their success, an endless chain of anxiety about future results. Krishna does not ask us to stop acting or even stop planning. He asks us to release the grip of anticipation, to act fully while holding outcomes lightly.
Today, choose one task that normally causes you anxiety about results, perhaps a work presentation, a difficult conversation, or a creative project. Before beginning, consciously offer both the action and its outcome to something greater than your ego. Perform the task with full engagement, but notice when the mind starts calculating results. Each time it does, gently return to the present action. At days end, reflect: Did this shift bring any measure of peace? The teaching promises it will, not eventually, but anantaram, immediately.
